I was an AMD fanboy for years, and I'd love to go back to them, but "clock-for-clock," the problem they have these days is power consumption. With Intel, I can build really, really small, and still get big desktop compute power. With AMD, I need specialized cooling solutions if I want to get anywhere near that small, and between the extra heat from that and the beefier power supply I have to put in, I have ot rethink where i can put the thing.

AMD is getting there. And when I do my next big-box build, I'll probably go AMD just like I did last time. But for practically everything else, Intel has them beat, and they know it.

I think the biggest speculation was that most of their inefficiencies were due to their lithography. FinFet at 14nm may completely change this, but we shall see.

Sauce:

http://wccftech.com/amd-1416nm-arctic-islands-launching-summer-2016/

Zen is max 95w CPU and 6900k is a 140w chip. Not to mention a large part of AMD's problems with power usage on desktop stems from the fact that Piledriver is a big chip (over 300mm^2 for a CPU) and it's 32nm. And that's competing with things like a 14nm 120mm^2 chip. The larger a chip is and the bigger the process, the more power it uses.

There's a good graph of die sizes here: http://www.anandtech.com/show/8426/the-intel-haswell-e-cpu-review-core-i7-5960x-i7-5930k-i7-5820k-tested 6950k die size is 247mm^2: http://hothardware.com/reviews/intel-core-i7-6950x-extreme-edition-10-core-cpu-review-broadwell-e-arrives But see how FX 8350 (Vishera) is the same number of transistors as Ivy Bridge 4c, and that's counting the GPU on the Ivy Bridge. I haven't seen any official numbers for Zen die size, but I've seen speculation based on the leaked die shots. And it sounds like it'll be around half a Vishera in size, which means as long as 14nm Global Foundaries is close to14nm Intel in power consumption, it should be pretty competitive in power consumption. 50% smaller than Vishera means about 160mm^2, much smaller than the Intel 6950k. One of AMD's big pushes with Zen is a physically small CPU core. Which makes it cheaper to produce and use less power. The big drawback to a smaller core is it's usually a lot slower than larger cores, but it looks like AMD managed to get a physically small core to perform very well.

Only thing is there is always going to be software that hurts AMD's performance, it's why this test uses Blender. It can be compiled neutrally without bullshit like Intel Compiler intentionally crippling AMD hardware by having the compiler generate code that checks if it's an AMD and then not run performance enhancing instructions like higher version SSE. The best way to use AMD hardware is in Linux, preferably in a distribution where you can compile performance sensitive programs, like Arch or Gentoo (or derivatives of them).

I'm cautiously optimistic. But AMD is making the right moves here and not doing anything high risk, like what they did with Bulldozer and it's radically different clustered design. As of now, there's no reason to think that Zen will use more power, in fact there's only reason to think it'll use less. But my main concern is that it won't clock to high frequencies, and I've yet to see anything persuade me otherwise. And that should be the primary worry. But as the article mentions, AMD is going to keep final clockspeeds quiet for a while because Zen is so close in performance per clock to Broadwell, and keeping that secret to the last minute means AMD can adjust them and have a slight lead. And the fact that we're even having to discuss AMD playing these games for CPUs is astounding, considering where they've been with Vishera.
